messages.author: eceaf8d32dda4993
messages.subject: Data results
parts:
Hey everyone,

I have just successfully run the distance program and found that my abundance results are the same as the number of individuals I spotted in the field. Does this mean in terms of my data? Could this mean there is something wrong with my code and or data? I tried it using both half-normal and uniform in the key function.

A sample of my distance R-code is:
hs<-read.csv("hs_rcode_com.csv")
attach(hs)
head(hs)
hscheck <- checkdata(hs)
hsh<-hscheck$data
region <- hscheck$region.table
sample <- hscheck$sample.table
obs <- hscheck$obs.table
head(hsh)
fhs <- ds(hsh, truncation = list(left= 0, right=50), transect = "point", formula=~1, key= c("unif"), adjustment = c("cos"), dht.group = FALSE, region.table = region, sample.table = sample, obs.table = obs,convert.units = 1, method = "nlminb", quiet = FALSE, debug.level = 0,
         initial.values = NULL)
summary(fhs)

A sample of my data tables for this code are:
species object Region.Label Area Sample.Label distance Effort detected observer
hs 1          h1.20 7853.98 1 29 1 1 1
hs 2          h1.20 7853.98 1 23 1 1 1
hs      h1.20 7853.98 1 29 1 1 1
hs 9              h1.120 7853.98 2 25 1 1 1
hs 10 h1.220 7853.98 3 12 1 1 1

Sorry for some odd reason object wouldn't go into the right place and the tables didn't format correctly

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Data results
parts:
Eric

The first suspect in answer to your question noting that abundance equals number seen is perhaps that the uniform key function you fitted to your data has not required the use of the cosine adjustment term you requested.  Recognise that ds() will fit a key function without adjustment terms, then the key with adjustment terms and perform an AIC comparison between them to decide whether the adjustment is warranted.  Check to see if that is the case with your data.

Next thing to do is simply plot your data.  Does your histogram of detections by distance have the characteristic "hump" shape, or does it continue to rise at large distances?  Plotting tells you lots about where potential problems might lie.

Not sure why you are going through the pain of creating "object", "detected" and "observer" fields in your data; I trust this is single observer data.  If they are single observer data, you should be able to use the "flatfile" data format as described.  Look at the help for the Distance package under 'flatfile.'  You can also have a quick look at the supplement to the Buckland et al. (2015) book where I have reanalysed Buckland's (2006) robin point count data.

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/DS.M&A/montrave/montrave-analysis.pdf

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Data results
parts:
That is an unfortunate situation, Eric.

One possible cause is animal movement.  The area associated with the outer-most bins of point transects is large.  If animals are moving through your points, they might be detected in those outer bands; giving rise to the phenomenon in your data.  The longer the duration of your "snapshot" count, the more individuals accumulate in the outer bands.  Have a look at Buckland's (2006) Auk paper about point transect sampling methodology.

If you measured the time during your count when detections were made, you might be able to truncate detections made after some number of minutes; reducing the effect of animal movement through your point stations.  Other than that, I don't know of a "normalisation" method to employ.
